interfaces.name: GPIO
interfaces.title: GPIO: General Purpose Input/Output
interfaces.text:
A GPIO pin can be read as an input, driven as an output, or switched to one of its alternate functions, connecting it to a peripheral inside the chip. On a Raspberry Pi 5 the header's 28 GPIO pins belong to the RP1 chip.

## Logic levels

GPIO pins are 3.3v. They are not 5v tolerant and could be damaged by 5v devices: use a level shifter, a divider or an optocoupler.

## Current

Treat an output as a control signal: anything that needs powering should be fed from the 3v3 or 5v pins, or from its own supply. [Raspberry Pi's GPIO documentation](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html#gpio) gives no per-pin or total limit for the header.

## Pull-ups and pull-downs

Every GPIO pin has an internal pull-up and pull-down resistor that can be enabled in software. GPIO 2 and GPIO 3 are the exception, with fixed 1.8 kΩ pull-ups fitted to the board.

At power-on, GPIO 0 to GPIO 8 are pulled up and GPIO 9 to GPIO 27 are pulled down. A relay board that switches on when its input is low can click on while the Pi starts if it's on a pulled-down pin, so CoilGate suggests GPIO 5 to 8 for those.

## Alternate functions

Pi 5's RP1 has nine alternate functions per pin, F0 to F8. Select a pin to see all of them. Overlays written before Pi 5 still work; the RP1 driver translates the old function numbers to the closest matching RP1 function.

## Checking a pin

`pinctrl get 17` shows what GPIO 17 is doing right now: input or output (`ip`, `op`), its pull (`pu`, `pd`) and level (`hi`, `lo`). Leave the pins CoilGate uses out of `gpio=` lines in /boot/firmware/config.txt, so the two don't fight over them.

interfaces.name: 3v3 Power
interfaces.title: 3v3 Power
interfaces.text:
All Raspberry Pi models since the B+ can provide up to 500mA on the 3v3 pins, thanks to a switching regulator. In some cases it may be possible to draw more but, due to lack of documentation and testing on the actual limits, 500mA is given as a rule of thumb.

The 5v supply coupled with a 3v3 regulator is recommended for powering 3.3v projects.

CoilGate's relay wiring takes the relay board's input-side VCC from pin 1, so a 5v relay board never puts more than 3.3v on a GPIO pin.

interfaces.name: 5v Power
interfaces.title: 5v Power
interfaces.text:
The 5v power pins are connected directly to the Pi's power input and will capably provide the full supply current of your power adaptor, minus that used by the Pi itself.

How much that leaves varies with the adaptor and what else is plugged in. On a Pi 5, use the official 27W (5v, 5A) supply if anything is powered from these pins. Devices that require a high current, such as LED panels, long LED strips, motors or a bank of relays, should use an external power supply.

interfaces.name: Ground
interfaces.title: Ground
interfaces.text:
The Ground pins on the Raspberry Pi are all electrically connected, so it doesn't matter which one you use if you're wiring up a voltage supply.

Generally the one that's most convenient or closest to the rest of your connections is tidier and easier, or alternatively the one closest to the supply pin that you use.

For example, it's a good idea to use Physical Pin 17 for 3v3 and Physical Pin 25 for ground when using the SPI connections, as these are right next to the important pins for SPI0.

interfaces.name: I²C
interfaces.title: I²C: Inter-Integrated Circuit
interfaces.text:
GPIO 2 and GPIO 3, the Raspberry Pi's I2C1 pins, allow for two-wire communication with a variety of external sensors and devices.

The I2C pins include a fixed 1.8 kΩ pull-up resistor to 3.3v. They are not suitable for use as general purpose IO where a pull-up might interfere.

I2C is a multi-drop bus: multiple devices can be connected to these same two pins. Each device has its own unique I2C address.

I2C is turned off on a stock Raspberry Pi OS image. Enable it with `raspi-config`, or by adding `dtparam=i2c_arm=on` to `/boot/firmware/config.txt`. Once it's on, `i2cdetect -y 1` from the `i2c-tools` package lists the addresses responding on the bus. CoilGate's BME280 sensors use this bus.

GPIO 0 and GPIO 1 (I2C0) can be used as an alternate I2C bus, but are typically used by the system to read the HAT EEPROM.

## More than one bus

i2c1 is the only bus available without an overlay. Pi 5 has several more, each on a pair of low-numbered GPIO pins:

| Pins | Pi 5 | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPIO 0 and GPIO 1 | i2c0 | Usually left alone for the HAT EEPROM |
| GPIO 2 and GPIO 3 | i2c1 | The usual bus |
| GPIO 4 and GPIO 5 | i2c2 | |
| GPIO 6 and GPIO 7 | i2c3 | |
| GPIO 8 and GPIO 9 | i2c0 | |
| GPIO 10 and GPIO 11 | i2c1 | |
| GPIO 12 and GPIO 13 | i2c2 | |
| GPIO 14 and GPIO 15 | i2c3 | Also the UART pins |
| GPIO 22 and GPIO 23 | i2c3 | |

Each bus is enabled with a device tree overlay, and the pin pair is chosen with a parameter. On Pi 5 the overlays take a `-pi5` suffix: `dtoverlay=i2c3-pi5,pins_6_7`.

Only GPIO 2 and GPIO 3 have pull-up resistors fitted. Every other pair needs your own, typically 4.7 kΩ to 3.3v.

interfaces.name: SPI
interfaces.title: SPI: Serial Peripheral Interface
interfaces.text:
* SPI0 pins are GPIO 7, GPIO 8, GPIO 9, GPIO 10 and GPIO 11
* SPI1 pins are GPIO 16, GPIO 17, GPIO 18, GPIO 19, GPIO 20 and GPIO 21

Known as the four-wire serial bus, SPI lets you attach multiple compatible devices to a single set of pins by assigning them different chip-select pins. To talk to an SPI device, you assert its corresponding chip-select pin.

SPI0 is off by default. Enable it with `raspi-config` or `dtparam=spi=on`; it then uses chip selects CE0 on GPIO 8 and CE1 on GPIO 7. You can enable SPI1 with a device tree overlay, for example `dtoverlay=spi1-3cs`.

## More than two buses

Pi 5 has extra SPI controllers on the low-numbered GPIO pins. Enable one with the matching overlay, in a `1cs` or `2cs` form for the number of chip selects you need, such as `dtoverlay=spi3-1cs-pi5`. The `cs0_pin` parameter moves the chip select if the default clashes with something.

Raspberry Pi 5 documentation calls MISO and MOSI SIO1 and SIO0, since RP1's SPI blocks can run in modes where the data lines change direction.

interfaces.name: UART
interfaces.title: UART: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter
interfaces.text:
UART is an asynchronous serial communication protocol: it takes bytes of data and transmits the individual bits one after another.

* TXD: Transmit
* RXD: Receive
* CTS: Clear to send
* RTS: Request to send

The UART pins are 3.3v and are not level shifted. Wire them straight to a 5v device and you might conjure up some magic blue smoke, so use a level shifter or a USB to 3.3v serial adaptor.

On Pi 5, the primary UART is the dedicated three-pin debug header, not GPIO 14 and GPIO 15. Set `enable_uart=1` in `/boot/firmware/config.txt` to bring the console back to the header pins.

Pi 5 exposes four more UARTs on the header:

| Pi 5 | TXD | RXD | CTS | RTS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| uart1 | GPIO 0 | GPIO 1 | GPIO 2 | GPIO 3 |
| uart2 | GPIO 4 | GPIO 5 | GPIO 6 | GPIO 7 |
| uart3 | GPIO 8 | GPIO 9 | GPIO 10 | GPIO 11 |
| uart4 | GPIO 12 | GPIO 13 | GPIO 14 | GPIO 15 |

These are enabled with a device tree overlay, such as `dtoverlay=uart1-pi5`, and the CTS/RTS pins with an additional `ctsrts` parameter.

interfaces.name: PWM
interfaces.title: PWM: Pulse-width Modulation
interfaces.text:
Pulse-width modulation creates a rectangular wave signal that is commonly used for dimming or blinking an LED, controlling a display backlight or the speed of a motor (e.g. a fan). The outputs are only useful as control signals, not to actually drive a motor.

On Pi 5 the RP1 PWM block has four channels: CHAN0 on GPIO 12, CHAN1 on GPIO 13, CHAN2 on GPIO 14 or GPIO 18, and CHAN3 on GPIO 15 or GPIO 19.

## Enable via config.txt

`dtoverlay=pwm` sets up one channel and `dtoverlay=pwm-2chan` sets up two, on GPIO 18 and GPIO 19 by default. The `pin` and `func` parameters move a channel to another of its pins:

```
dtoverlay=pwm-2chan,pin=12,func=4,pin2=13,func2=4
```

`func` is the function number for the pin you pick: 4 for GPIO 12 and GPIO 13, 2 for GPIO 18 and GPIO 19. These are the numbers the older models use, and they still work on Pi 5, where the RP1 GPIO driver maps each one to the closest matching RP1 function.

GPIO 18 and GPIO 19 are also the I2S clock and frame select, which makes GPIO 12 and GPIO 13 the pair to use alongside an I2S audio HAT. Pi 5 also has `dtoverlay=pwm-pio`, which drives a PWM signal from PIO on any GPIO pin rather than from the PWM block.

interfaces.name: PCM / I²S
interfaces.title: PCM / I²S: Digital audio
interfaces.text:
PCM (Pulse-code Modulation) is a digital representation of sampled analog. On the Raspberry Pi it's a form of digital audio which can be understood by a DAC for high quality sound.

These are the pins you'll want for I2S (Inter-IC Sound), which is the signalling most audio HATs and DACs use and the name they usually give it: clock on GPIO 18, frame select on GPIO 19, data in on GPIO 20 and data out on GPIO 21. Pi 5's RP1 adds extra data lines on GPIO 22 to GPIO 27.

I2S is off by default. `dtparam=i2s=on` in /boot/firmware/config.txt enables it, though most audio HATs ship an overlay that does this as part of their own setup.

interfaces.name: GPCLK
interfaces.title: GPCLK: General Purpose Clock
interfaces.text:
General Purpose Clock pins can be set up to output a fixed frequency without any ongoing software control.

On Pi 5, GPCLK0 is available on GPIO 4 or GPIO 20, GPCLK1 on GPIO 5, GPIO 18 or GPIO 21, and GPCLK2 on GPIO 6. RP1's clock sources differ from the older models', so frequency tables written for Pi 4 and earlier don't apply.

interfaces.name: 1-Wire
interfaces.title: 1-Wire
interfaces.text:
One-wire is a single-wire communication bus typically used to connect sensors to the Pi, such as the DS18B20 temperature probes CoilGate reads.

The Raspberry Pi supports one-wire on any GPIO pin, but the default is GPIO 4.

## Enable via config.txt

Add the overlay to /boot/firmware/config.txt and reboot, or let `raspi-config` do it for you:

```
dtoverlay=w1-gpio
```

Any other pin needs the `gpiopin` parameter, for example `dtoverlay=w1-gpio,gpiopin=17`. Devices found on the bus appear in `/sys/bus/w1/devices/`.

Using w1-gpio on the Raspberry Pi typically needs a 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor connected between the GPIO pin and a 3.3v supply (e.g. header pin 1 or 17).

interfaces.name: SDIO
interfaces.title: SDIO: SD card interface
interfaces.text:
SDIO is the SD host interface. Its signals are normally used for the microSD slot, but a second four-bit SD interface can be brought out on GPIO 22 to GPIO 27.

Pi 5 has its own overlay for this, `dtoverlay=sdio-pi5`, which uses these six pins.

interfaces.name: DPI
interfaces.title: DPI: Display Parallel Interface
interfaces.text:
DPI drives a parallel RGB display directly from the GPIO pins: a pixel clock, data enable, horizontal and vertical sync, and up to 24 data bits. In its widest mode it uses every GPIO pin on the header, leaving nothing else free.

It's enabled with a display overlay in /boot/firmware/config.txt. See [Raspberry Pi's DPI documentation](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html#display-parallel-interface-dpi) for the modes and overlays.

interfaces.name: PIO
interfaces.title: PIO: Programmable I/O (Pi 5)
interfaces.text: New on Pi 5: RP1 has a PIO block, like the one in the Raspberry Pi Pico, that runs small programs to generate or read signals on any GPIO pin. Overlays such as `pwm-pio` use it, and it can implement interfaces the other blocks don't have.

interfaces.name: JTAG / SWD
interfaces.title: JTAG and SWD
interfaces.text:
Pi 5's 40-pin header doesn't carry a JTAG interface of its own; debugging the Pi 5 itself uses its dedicated debug connector.

A Pi can be the debugger rather than the target. OpenOCD bit-bangs JTAG or SWD over the GPIO pins highlighted here:

| Signal | GPIO | Header |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCK / SWCLK | GPIO 11 | Physical Pin 23 |
| TMS / SWDIO | GPIO 8 | Physical Pin 24 |
| TDI | GPIO 10 | Physical Pin 19 |
| TDO | GPIO 9 | Physical Pin 21 |
| TRST | GPIO 7 | Physical Pin 26 |
| SRST | GPIO 24 | Physical Pin 18 |

SWD needs only SWCLK and SWDIO. TRST and SRST are optional. You also need a ground connection, and Physical Pin 20 is conveniently in amongst the signals. These are the SPI0 pins, so SPI0 and OpenOCD cannot both be in use.

On Pi 5, pass `interface/raspberrypi5-gpiod.cfg` to OpenOCD. Pi 5 needs its own file because the GPIO pins hang off the RP1 chip across PCIe, out of reach of the native bit-bang driver. It falls back to the generic Linux gpiod driver, which is slower and has no adjustable clock speed.
